catalog_quote: Upper Asaro may be described as having a two-tone system. However, it would be more accurate to speak of tone areas than of tone levels. While the two tones, HIGH and LOW carry the meaning, they are not perturbed by other influences, but may be modified. ... The theories presented here have been made from a study of two-syllable and three-syllable nouns, spot checked on modifiers and pronouns. The possible pressure of grammar on tone-stress patterns for Asaro verbs has not been done. 1.1 Tone (and not stress) as a phonemic feature of Asaro may be demonstrated by several ‘tone pairs’. ... 'vélè mouth-his cf. vè'lè eye-his; ... 'gúhè a pine cf. gù'hè a grass. ('gókà your nose cf. gò'kà your bag.) à'kà ladder cf. à'ká road. à'ngálè young of animals cf. à'ngàlè a pine. Because of the tendency of English speakers to equate high tone and stress, à'kà vs à'ká and à'ngálè vs à'ngàlè become difficult to hear. A two syllable word with two possible tones may fit any of 4 mathematical ‘tone patterns’. A three syllable word with two possible tones may fit any of 8 different mathematical patterns. Asaro has words fitting all but one possible ‘tone pattern’. The stress, for words without glottal, may be predicted. Stress falls on the first high tone in a word; otherwise on the second low tone. TWO SYLLABLE: High-High 'mbéné a banana ... High-Low 'vánì old man ... Low-Low gò'vì sweet potato ... Low-High à'ká road

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dano (Upper Asaro) has two lexical tones (High/Low); stress is not phonemic but predictable from the tone pattern: in words without a glottal stop, stress falls on the first High-toned syllable; in all-Low words it falls on the second syllable (e.g. 'mbéné, 'vánì, à'ká, gò'vì; 'vólíhé, gà'tànà, mì'súmbó). Syllables closed by glottal stop are shorter, higher and more forceful and are excluded from the rule pending further study.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule stated only 'for words without glottal' (glottal-closed syllables get 'more force', 1.4.c, to be studied further); generalisations drawn from 2- and 3-syllable nouns, spot-checked on modifiers and pronouns; 'tone-stress patterns for Asaro verbs' not studied; one Low-High-Low set (gǎvózò etc.) is listed without a stress mark.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms of nouns (isolated words and short tone frames); authors note utterance-level intonation lowers final unstressed syllables and that stressed Low syllables are raised within the Low register (1.4.b). The later OPD (Strange 1992) records only 'two phonemic tones' and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Upper Asaro = Dano [aso] (dano1240) as spoken around Kasena/Kofena, Goroka district; the 1974 ms. says its tone/stress generalisations were made from 2- and 3-syllable nouns (spot-checked on modifiers and pronouns), verbs not studied. No dialect split relevant.

sources.note: Two-tone system (HIGH/LOW 'tone areas'); 'Tone (and not stress)' is the phonemic feature, shown by tone pairs; stress is predictable for words without glottal stop: 'Stress falls on the first high tone in a word; otherwise on the second low tone' (p.2), with stress-marked 2- and 3-syllable noun lists by tone pattern (pp.2-3); stressed low syllables are raised within the low area, glottal-closed syllables get 'more force' (p.4).
